title: Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier: Field Experimental Evidence of the Effects of AI on Knowledge Worker Productivity and Quality
pub: Harvard Business School Technology & Operations Mgt. Unit Working Paper No. 24-013 (SSRN 4573321); version of record: Organization Science (2026), DOI 10.1287/orsc.2025.21838
author: Fabrizio Dell'Acqua · Edward McFowland III · Ethan Mollick · Hila Lifshitz-Assaf · Katherine C. Kellogg · Saran Rajendran · Lisa Krayer · François Candelon · Karim R. Lakhani

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Professional power: AI redistributes tasks and status
st.an: The supplied excerpts are bibliography-only and provide no substantive argument, evidence, findings, predictions or recommendations from the source. Its position on whether AI redistributes legal tasks and professional status through organisational choices and professional power therefore cannot be determined.

st.t: Assisted inequality: Productivity gains need not improve careers
st.an: The source reinforces the cluster’s outcome-specific account of AI productivity and materially develops it through the jagged-capability-frontier framework: GPT-4 substantially improved speed, completion and quality on suitable consulting tasks, yet reduced correctness outside its capabilities. It does not establish employment, income or career effects, but shows why assisted performance cannot be treated as uniformly beneficial.
qs: For each one of a set of 18 realistic consulting tasks within the frontier of AI capabilities, consultants using AI were significantly more productive (they completed 12.2% more tasks on average, and completed tasks 25.1% more quickly), and produced significantly higher quality results (more than 40% higher quality compared to a control group).
For a task selected to be outside the frontier, however, consultants using AI were 19 percentage points less likely to produce correct solutions compared to those without AI.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source materially strengthens the cluster with randomized evidence that AI improves speed and quality on suitable professional tasks but degrades correctness beyond its capability frontier. It also extends the cluster’s competence-risk proposition by warning that diverting junior work may create training deficits and by emphasizing expertise, verification and task-specific human–AI workflow design. Its evidence concerns consulting rather than legal practice, so the legal implications are transferable rather than directly tested.
qs: Our results demonstrate that AI capabilities cover an expanding, but uneven, set of knowledge work we call a "jagged technological frontier.” Within this growing frontier, AI can complement or even displace human work; outside of the frontier, AI output is inaccurate, less useful, and degrades human performance.

st.t: Practical productivity: AI can save or consume time
st.an: The source materially develops the cluster’s proposition through randomized experiments comparing unaided and GPT-4-assisted knowledge work across deliberately different task types. It provides direct evidence that productivity and quality effects depend on whether a task falls within GPT-4’s uneven capability frontier, while also limiting some timing conclusions through its experimental design.
qs: Our results show that this generation of LLMs are highly capable of causing significant increases in quality and productivity, or even completely automating some tasks, but the actual tasks that AI can do are surprising and not immediately obvious to individuals or even to producers of LLMs themselves.
The second experiment was designed so that GPT-4 would make an error when conducting the analysis, ensuring the work fell just outside the frontier.

st.t: Productivity distribution: Weaker users do not always gain most
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core conditionality and materially develops it with randomized evidence: weaker consultants gained more on tasks within AI’s capability frontier, while AI reduced correctness on a task outside that frontier. It therefore shows why productivity distribution depends on task-level capability, workflow design and verification rather than access alone.
qs: Consultants across the skills distribution benefited significantly from having AI augmentation, with those below the average performance threshold increasing by 43% and those above increasing by 17% compared to their own scores.
For a task selected to be outside the frontier, however, consultants using AI were 19 percentage points less likely to produce correct solutions compared to those without AI.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source directly substantiates the cluster’s core proposition with randomized field evidence that AI produces large gains on some knowledge-work tasks but degrades correctness on others. It materially develops the synthesis by defining the jagged capability frontier and recommending task-level human–AI configurations, verification and continued investment in expertise rather than blanket adoption or substitution.
qs: Our results demonstrate that AI capabilities cover an expanding, but uneven, set of knowledge work we call a "jagged technological frontier.” Within this growing frontier, AI can complement or even displace human work; outside of the frontier, AI output is inaccurate, less useful, and degrades human performance.

The results suggest that this debate should move beyond the dichotomous decision of adopting or not AI and instead focus on the knowledge workflow and the tasks within it, and in each of them, evaluate the value of using different configurations and combinations of humans and AI.

st.t: Creative diversity: Individual gains can homogenise groups
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s central distinction between individual performance gains and collective idea diversity: it reports an association between greater AI-output retention and better answers while separately investigating variation across participants’ ideas. However, the supplied excerpt reports no diversity outcome, so it supports the analytical framing rather than establishing homogenisation or evaluating personas as mitigation.
qs: Either way, what is clear is that those who choose to retain to a relatively high degree produced significantly better answers on average, and that this certainly can have a profound impact on how organizations consider the use of GenerativeAI technologies by their employees.

This question is motivated by various debates on the impact of GenerativeAI on firms, including how the ability for GenerativeAI to increase the productivity of individual employees translates to overall improvements for the firm.

st.t: Knowledge work: Task gains do not ensure skill growth
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s core distinction between demonstrated task-level gains and uniform productivity claims: it reports substantial quality and productivity benefits for suitable tasks while emphasizing that knowledge-work tasks differ sharply in AI suitability and that impacts will be uneven. It does not directly assess durable skill formation or whole-job replacement.
qs: Most knowledge work includes this sort of flow, a set of interdependent tasks, some of which may be good fit for current AI, while some are not.

Our results show that this generation of LLMs are highly capable of causing significant increases in quality and productivity, or even completely automating some tasks, but the actual tasks that AI can do are surprising and not immediately obvious to individuals or even to producers of LLMs themselves.

st.t: Legal productivity: Speed gains exceed quality gains
st.an: The study supports the cluster’s task- and baseline-dependent account: GPT-4 improved completion, quality and speed on work inside its capability frontier, with substantially larger performance gains for relatively lower-ranked participants. Its constrained timing measure also reinforces the cluster’s caution against treating reported speed gains as a universal productivity multiplier, though it does not itself show that speed gains exceeded quality gains.
qs: When comparing the two groups, though, we see the bottom- half-skill performers exhibited the most substantial surge in performance, 43%, compared to the top-half-skill subjects, 17%.

kp.k: Randomized consulting experiments test GPT-4 augmentation
kp.d: The authors report two pre-registered randomized experiments conducted in Spring 2023 with 758 BCG strategy consultants, about 7% of the firm's individual contributor consultants. Of these, 385 undertook product-development tasks and 373 undertook business problem-solving tasks, with no overlap between groups. Following an unaided baseline assessment, participants received no AI, GPT-4 access, or GPT-4 access plus a prompt-engineering overview. This is evidence about consulting knowledge work, not a direct study of legal services.
qs: The study encompassed 758 strategy consultants, each of whom completed the initial survey and experimental tasks.
Each participant was assigned to one of two distinct experiments.
All subjects used the same version of the tool, accessing GPT-4 as available at the end of April, 2023, and using default system prompts and temperature.

kp.k: AI capability varies within individual knowledge workflows
kp.d: The authors propose a jagged technological frontier: tasks appearing similarly difficult can fall on opposite sides of AI's capabilities, so AI can improve or impair performance within the same workflow. They argue that organizations should assess task-level combinations of human and AI work rather than treat adoption as a binary decision. The frontier is presented as changing with technology, not as a permanent classification of tasks.
qs: Tasks with the same perceived difficulty may be on one side or the other of the frontier.
We found that the utility of AI can fluctuate over the course of a professional’s workflow, with some tasks falling inside while others fall outside of the frontier.

kp.k: Within-frontier tasks show substantial quality and completion gains
kp.d: Across 18 footwear product-development tasks covering creativity, analysis, writing and persuasion, AI improved quality and task completion. The abstract reports 12.2% more tasks completed and more than 40% higher quality. Table 1's primary human-graded specification reports quality increases of 42.5% with the overview and 38% with GPT alone, relative to a control mean of 4.099. Completion averaged approximately 93% and 91%, respectively, against 82% for controls. The paper also contains a later 12.5% completion summary, rather than the 12.2% reported in the abstract and main completion discussion.
qs: In Column 1, GPT + Overview leads to a 1.75 increase in scores over the control mean of 4.1, which is a 42.5% increase; GPT Only led to a 1.56, or 38% increase.
The control group completed on average 82% of their tasks, while the GPT + Overview condition completed about 93% and GPT Only about 91%.

kp.k: Speed gains concern reaching the final question
kp.d: The abstract reports that AI users completed tasks 25.1% more quickly. For the within-frontier experiment, participants could not finish the exercise before its allotted time, so the timing measure was seconds taken to reach the final question after completing the first 17. Table 3 reports reductions of 1129.143 seconds with the overview and 1388.415 seconds with GPT alone, against a control mean of 5023 seconds. These results should be distinguished from reductions in total session duration.
qs: For the task inside the frontier, we did not allow any subjects to complete the task before the allotted time was over.
The dependent variable represents the total seconds taken to reach the final question.

kp.k: Lower baseline performers gain more from augmentation
kp.d: Among AI-treated consultants, the bottom half of the baseline performance distribution improved by 43% relative to their own assessment scores, compared with 17% for the top half. These are within-person comparisons across comparable assessment and experimental tasks, not the same comparison as treatment versus control. The authors interpret the results as both raising performance and narrowing performance differences, while emphasizing that even the relatively lower-performing consultants were highly skilled.
qs: When comparing the two groups, though, we see the bottom- half-skill performers exhibited the most substantial surge in performance, 43%, compared to the top-half-skill subjects, 17%.
All these consultants would appear to be extremely high-skill in most other real-world contexts.

kp.k: Outside-frontier AI use reduces decision correctness
kp.d: The researchers deliberately designed a business case requiring interview insights to reinterpret spreadsheet data, such that GPT-4 would struggle without extensive guidance. Controls answered correctly about 84.5% of the time, versus about 60% with GPT plus overview and 70% with GPT alone: an average reduction of 19 percentage points. Table 4's unadjusted coefficients are −0.245 and −0.139, respectively. This is a finding about correctness on the selected case, not a general model hallucination rate.
qs: Our goal was to design a task where consultants would excel, but AI would struggle without extensive guidance.

Subjects in the control group were correct about this exercise about 84.5% of the time, while the AI conditions scored at 60% and 70% (for an average decrease of 19 percentage points when combining the AI treatment conditions and comparing them to the control condition).

kp.k: Better-rated recommendations can accompany incorrect decisions
kp.d: On the outside-frontier case, AI reduced time spent while increasing human-graded recommendation quality, despite reducing correctness. The unadjusted recommendation-quality gains were 25.1% with the overview and 17.9% with GPT alone; gains were also observed separately among correct and incorrect answers. The authors distinguish the quality of the recommendations from whether the underlying business choice was correct.
qs: Across all specifications, subjects using AI (both GPT + Overview and GPT Only) consistently outperformed those not using AI in terms of recommendation quality, regardless of the correctness of their answer.
That is, the quality of the recommendation about a business problem-solving case increased, regardless of whether the underlying recommendation was correct or not.

kp.d: The prompt-engineering overview produced greater quality improvements than GPT access alone inside the frontier, but the outside-frontier overview group had a larger correctness decline and greater time reduction. The between-treatment correctness difference reached the 10% significance threshold, not the conventional 5% threshold. The authors also associate the overview with increased retention of AI text, while leaving the underlying mechanism unresolved.
qs: Specifically, the GPT + Overview treatment consistently exhibits a more pronounced positive effect compared to the GPT Only treatment.
When directly comparing the two treatments, the difference in their impacts is statistically significant at the 10% threshold across specifications.

kp.k: Text retention does not establish abdication of judgment
kp.d: Appendix C measures retention using normalized character-edit similarity between submitted answers and AI responses in the creative experiment. Modal average retention was approximately 0.87, and higher retention was associated with higher answer quality. However, the authors explicitly caution that near-copying could follow careful iterative prompting rather than uncritical reliance; their analysis cannot distinguish these mechanisms. This association does not establish that removing human judgment causes better performance.
qs: Alternatively, a subject could be engaging in “high-quality” prompting behavior, e.g., helping ChatGPT to iteratively refine its responses until it is perfected, and only then retaining a high amount of the response in their answers.
Currently, our analysis cannot distinguish between the two, and in general, it is not straightforward how to assess prompting quality.

kp.k: Higher individual quality accompanies reduced collective idea diversity
kp.d: Using Google's Universal Sentence Encoder to compare shoe ideas across participants, the authors find that AI-assisted idea lists were higher-rated but more semantically similar. A supplementary simulation of 100 independent ChatGPT sessions showed still greater similarity. They caution that this does not establish the same pattern for each participant's best ideas or all users. Multiple models and more human-only involvement are proposed as possible countermeasures, not tested remedies.
qs: This suggests that while GPT-4 aids in generating superior content, it might lead to more homogenized outputs.
Simply because the full set of 10 ideas for subjects with access to ChatGPT is generally of higher quality and less variable does not imply the best idea(s) for each subject follow this same pattern.

kp.k: Centaur and cyborg practices describe emerging collaboration patterns
kp.d: Exploratory analysis identifies centaurs, who allocate work between human and AI strengths, and cyborgs, who integrate both at granular subtask level through iterative interaction. Appendix E examines 244 AI-using consultants on the analytic task and notes that the same person could use both approaches. These are emerging observational categories, not experimentally established rankings of collaboration strategies; their effects on performance remain under investigation.
qs: Users with this strategy switch between AI and human tasks, allocating responsibilities based on the strengths and capabilities of each entity.
Cyborg users don’t just delegate tasks; they intertwine their efforts with AI at the very frontier of capabilities.
We are also investigating the impact of these behaviors on performance.

kp.k: Expert judgment and future training remain organizational concerns
kp.d: The authors recommend continued cognitive effort, interrogation of AI output and expert judgment, particularly outside the capability frontier. They warn that diverting suitable work away from juniors could create long-term training deficits and argue that frontier-navigation expertise must be developed through education, workplace training and employee upskilling. The junior-training deficit is a prospective organizational risk, not an outcome measured by these experiments.
qs: Professionals who had a negative performance when using AI tended to blindly adopt its output and interrogate it less (“unengaged interaction with AI” Lebovitz et al. (2022)).
An immediate danger emerging from these findings, for instance, is that people will stop delegating work inside the frontier to junior workers, creating long-term training deficits (Beane, 2019).

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Dell’Acqua and coauthors claim that GPT-4 improves consulting work within its capabilities but can reduce correctness outside them; they also identify implications for collaboration, idea diversity, and training.
pts.d: This is a cross-domain study of management consultants, not a study of legal services. The authors report that, across 18 consulting tasks within GPT-4’s capability frontier, AI users completed 12.2% more tasks, took 25.1% less time to reach the final question, and produced work summarized as more than 40% higher quality. The principal human-scored composite estimates were 42.5% higher with GPT plus an overview and 38% higher with GPT alone. Below-median baseline performers improved by 43% and above-median performers by 17% relative to their own assessment scores. On a business-analysis task designed to lie outside GPT-4’s frontier, AI access reduced correctness by approximately 19 percentage points. Nevertheless, AI users completed that task faster and received higher recommendation-quality scores even when their underlying answer was wrong. The authors describe two emerging collaboration practices: 'Centaurs' divide work between humans and AI, whereas 'Cyborgs' integrate their contributions at a granular level. They also report reduced collective diversity of AI-assisted ideas. Broader forward-looking claims include possible automation of some tasks, reduced delegation to juniors and consequent training deficits, and potentially lower costs of thinking and reasoning. These broader implications are not measured employment or market outcomes.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The performance claims rest on two preregistered randomized experiments; collaboration mechanisms and longer-term organizational implications have a more exploratory or prospective basis.
pts.d: The study involved 758 BCG individual-contributor consultants, approximately 7% of that population at the firm: 385 undertook product-development tasks and 373 undertook business-analysis tasks, with no overlap between the experimental samples. Participants first completed an unaided baseline assessment and then were randomly assigned to no AI, GPT-4, or GPT-4 plus a prompt-engineering overview. Tasks were developed with industry practitioners to resemble professional activities, and participation and performance were incentivized. Evidence included human grading, supplementary GPT-4 grading, binary correctness measures, completion rates, timing, and regression analyses. The timing measure for the inside-frontier experiment was time to reach question 18, not time to finish the entire exercise. Collective variation was measured using semantic similarity of shoe ideas, with an additional simulation of 100 independent ChatGPT sessions. The centaur/cyborg typology derives from exploratory analysis of interaction logs and qualitative evidence; the authors explicitly state that its performance implications were still being investigated. Textual retainment was associated with higher quality inside the frontier, but the authors caution that their measure cannot distinguish uncritical copying from retaining output after effective iterative prompting. Predictions concerning junior training, new roles, and broader cognitive costs are discussion-level extrapolations, not outcomes tested in the experiment.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The measured effects concern short experimental tasks using spring-2023 GPT-4; benefits depend on task fit, and the authors give no fixed timetable for broader changes.
pts.d: The supplied full text is the September 22, 2023 working paper, notwithstanding the later publication information in the document heading. The experiments used GPT-4 as available at the end of April 2023, through a company platform using the OpenAI API and default system prompts and temperature. Participants were invited to spend five hours on the experiment; the main inside-frontier exercise allowed 90 minutes and the outside-frontier exercise 60 minutes. The findings concern immediate performance rather than sustained workplace productivity or long-term learning. The outside-frontier task was deliberately constructed so that straightforward prompting would lead GPT-4 to an incorrect conclusion unless users supplied extensive guidance. The authors emphasize that apparently similar tasks can fall on different sides of the capability frontier and that the frontier changes as models improve. The prompt-engineering overview improved inside-frontier quality but did not eliminate outside-frontier errors: its correctness reduction was larger than that of GPT alone, with the treatment difference significant at the 10% threshold. The authors advocate continued expert judgment and checking of AI output. Their forecasts about training deficits, organizing work, and reduced cognitive costs have no quantified adoption schedule.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The directly studied population is highly skilled BCG consultants; the authors extend their implications to knowledge-work organizations, junior workers, and AI designers.
pts.d: Individual-contributor consultants receive task-dependent gains in speed, output quantity, and assessed quality, but can also make more incorrect decisions when relying on AI beyond its capabilities. Lower baseline performers gain more within the frontier, although both skill groups benefit and both consist of highly selected professionals. Employers face choices about dividing workflows between humans and AI, developing expertise in checking and challenging outputs, and balancing higher average idea quality against reduced collective variety. Junior workers may lose learning opportunities if AI replaces tasks previously delegated to them; this is a prospective risk rather than observed displacement. The authors also note that AI could support training. AI designers and companies are identified as actors who could improve tools and users’ ability to navigate capability boundaries. No direct effects on lawyers, legal clients, law-firm staffing, legal pricing, or access to justice are established by these experiments.
